source.title: Vision-by-Language for Training-Free Compositional Image Retrieval
source.authors: Shyamgopal Karthik; Karsten Roth; Massimiliano Mancini; Zeynep Akata

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present. Figure 6's plotted values are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether scale predicts downstream task performance using retrieval accuracy on image-retrieval benchmarks, rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study scales OpenCLIP retrieval models and reports resulting CIR performance. Other benchmark comparisons, component ablations, and cited language-model scaling results do not test the claim versions and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study swaps in LAION-2B OpenCLIP retrieval models from about 150M to 2.5B parameters inside a fixed captioner+LLM pipeline. It reports a 'clear log-linear relationship' between capacity and CIRCO/CIRR scores. That is a downstream-task scaling result in a new setting (contrastive vision-language retrievers on compositional retrieval), so it bears on V6. It is not T2: no LM loss and no LM downstream tasks are measured. No power-law loss fit, extrapolation, allocation, shape or fit-choice result is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that scaling the CLIP retrieval component substantially boosts CIR performance, with a clear log-linear capacity–performance relationship on CIRCO and CIRR that partly breaks the retrieval bottleneck. They also note this partly contrasts with the minimal scaling gains Vaze et al. (2023) found.
record.recipe_differences: Scales pretrained vision-language retrieval models and measures image-retrieval accuracy, rather than fitting language-model held-out loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Retrieval model capacity is varied; the reported outcome is CIRCO or CIRR performance. Individual model-size results are not stated in the text.
record.problems: The text does not provide individual points from the scale sweep, and no uncertainty estimates are stated. The reported scaling trend is limited to two image-retrieval benchmarks and does not establish a power law in language-model pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling results were left out. Non-scaling benchmark comparisons and component ablations do not test a listed version.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss is measured and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute is reported.
No fits on small runs are used to predict larger ones.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is studied.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Only downstream retrieval accuracy is scaled; the loss power-law form for image-text models is not measured (cites Cherti et al. only).

Untested: predictability from pretraining loss; any quantitative fit or extrapolation; language-model downstream tasks; scaling of the LLM or captioner components (LLM comparison mixes families, not a scale sweep).
No exponents, fitting choices or curve bending are examined.

missing.what: OpenAI-CLIP ViT-B/32 to ViT-L/14 comparison. CIRCO mAP@5 rises 14.94 to 18.57, but CIRR R@1 barely moves (23.94 to 24.55) before jumping to 34.65 with OpenCLIP ViT-G/14. Weights and training data differ across these points, which confounds size.
FashionIQ average R@10 rises 28.55 (ViT-L/14) to 32.19 (OpenCLIP ViT-G/14); the authors cite this as a benefit of scaling. It is a two-point comparison confounded by different weights.
GeneCIS average R@1 rises 15.9 (ViT-L/14) to 17.4 (OpenCLIP ViT-G/14), a small gain. Some subtasks (Focus Attribute, Focus Object) move little or fall versus ViT-B/32 or RN50x4.
Per-model points of the OpenCLIP scaling sweep.

record.verdict_notes: This is a methods paper on training-free compositional image retrieval, and scaling is a side analysis. The models scaled are contrastive vision-language retrievers, not language models, and the measure is downstream retrieval accuracy, not loss. V6 relevance therefore rests on a broad reading of 'downstream tasks improve predictably with scale'. The evidence is a qualitative statement about a figure, without fit statistics or uncertainty. Other model swaps (LLM choice, captioner) compare different families rather than scale sweeps, and no row should be added for them.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or power-law dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No power-law fits from small runs or predictions of larger runs are evaluated.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens is studied.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Image retrieval performance is scaled, but the study does not test whether the same power-law form holds for loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests retrieval performance versus model scale on CIRCO and CIRR only; it does not test predictability across other downstream tasks or from pretraining loss.
No fitting choices, exponents, compute-optimal splits, or curve bending are compared.

rows.value: A clear log-linear relationship between model capacity and performance is reported; performance reaches mAP@5 = 26.77%.
rows.locator: Section 4.3, “Investigating Scaling Laws for ZS-CIR,” Figure 6 and accompanying text
rows.note: The text gives the trend and maximum score but not the individual model-size measurements; the reported trend aggregates the scaling sweep.
rows.check: Baseline should be the smallest OpenCLIP model (~150M params), whose score is not given in text. Per-point values sit only in Figure 6. 26.77% mAP@5 is the ViT-G/14 test-set endpoint from Table 1. The trend is stated qualitatively, with no fitted slope or goodness of fit. The subject is a CLIP retriever, not a language model, so the V6 link holds only under a broad reading of 'downstream tasks'.
